report:
Based on the evidence, I can now confirm your assessment.

## Report

The claim that flu vaccination *causes* Alzheimer's disease is false, and the evidence actually points in the opposite direction.

Multiple large observational studies suggest flu vaccination is associated with *reduced*, not increased, Alzheimer's risk. A widely cited claims-based cohort study from UTHealth Houston, using propensity-score matching on nearly 2 million patients (935,887 vaccinated vs. 935,887 unvaccinated), found flu vaccination associated with roughly a 40% lower relative risk of developing Alzheimer's disease over four years (medicalxpress.com/news/2022-06-flu-vaccination-linked-alzheimer-disease.html). Follow-up work from the same group, published in the *Journal of Alzheimer's Disease*, extended this to other vaccines (Tdap/Td, shingles, pneumococcal), all similarly linked to lower Alzheimer's risk in adults 65+ (uth.edu/news/story/several-vaccines-associated-with-reduced-risk-of-alzheimers-disease-in-adults-65-and-older). A broader review in PMC likewise catalogs associations between various infections/vaccines and reduced dementia risk (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11060001/).

Importantly, these are observational, associational studies (not randomized trials), so they cannot prove vaccination *prevents* Alzheimer's — confounding by healthier vaccinated populations is possible. But nothing in this literature supports a causal harmful link; the direction of association is protective, not causative of disease.

Separately, fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar unfounded claims linking other vaccines (e.g., COVID-19 vaccines) to Alzheimer's/dementia, noting no credible scientific basis and problematic sourcing behind such claims (factcheck.afp.com/study-falsely-claims-covid-19-vaccines-may-cause-neurodegenerative-diseases; politifact.com/factchecks/2021/feb/26/j-bart-classen/coronavirus-vaccine-doesnt-cause-alzheimers-als/).

**Conclusion:** No credible evidence supports "flu vaccine causes Alzheimer's"; existing data suggest a protective association instead.
